---
title: "Comparing pulse-extraction methods on real videos"
subtitle: "Seven ways from a registered B-scan video to a cardiac phase, run over the whole SANSORI cohort — 107 conditions attempted, 106 usable, 14 subjects"
include-in-header: figures_pulse_from_data/plotlyjs.html
---

Every page before this one asks what an SVD does to an object we built
ourselves. This one asks the only question that ultimately matters: on **real**
registered B-scan videos, which of the available tools actually returns a usable
cardiac pulse — and at what price.

"Usable" is not a matter of taste here. The pulse is never the deliverable; the
**phase** is. Downstream, that phase folds the video into an averaged cardiac
cycle, from which choroidal thickness pulsatility and then the rigidity
coefficient $k$ are estimated. A method that recovers a beautiful heart rate but
a phase that is wrong at any given instant is worse than useless — it produces a
clean-looking one-cycle reconstruction of nothing. Keep that in mind when
reading the tables below: **rate accuracy and phase correctness are not the same
property**, and the results separate on exactly that point.

Every figure is interactive: hover a point to get the condition it belongs to,
drag to zoom, click a legend entry to isolate a series.

## What every method is given

All seven methods share one front end, computed once per condition, so that
nothing downstream can be blamed on a different input:

1. **ROI** — the central 3/4 of the A-scans (the lateral edges are where
   registration is least reliable) and the upper half of the local choroidal
   thickness (the Bruch's-membrane / choriocapillaris side). One pixel is one
   trace; no spatial pooling.
2. **Normalisation** — each frame divided by its own mean intensity, then the
   temporal mean removed from every trace.
3. **Decomposition** — SVD at **rank 100**, plus a Lomb–Scargle periodogram of
   every singular vector on the true, non-uniform acquisition timestamps.
4. **Channel selection** — the optimised spectral combination returns both a
   reference pulse and the list of singular components it considers cardiac.

The reference heart rate comes from `visit_data.csv` (ECG-derived) for all 106
usable conditions — the SVD-based fallback was never needed.

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/tab_cohort.qmd >}}

Two numbers in that table deserve attention. The **first triplet holds only 18 %
of the variance**: there is no dominant mode, the video is genuinely
high-dimensional. And the **resampling correlation of 0.93** is a cost, not a
diagnostic — SSA and the Hilbert transform both require a uniformly sampled
signal, so every method except the raw combination pays for one interpolation
from the real timestamps onto a uniform grid. The production pipeline avoids it
until the FIR stage; the SSA methods incur it immediately.

## The pulse is not in the leading components

Before comparing methods, one result decides the shape of the whole pipeline.

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f4_svd_map.qmd >}}

On this condition the components tagged cardiac are $v_{49}$ through $v_{83}$ —
and the largest weight in the combination goes to $v_{78}$. The leading
components, bright across the whole frequency axis on the left of the map, carry
broadband and low-frequency content: bulk motion, residual misregistration,
intensity drift. Not the heartbeat.

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f4b_channel_index.qmd >}}

This holds across the cohort. Of the 623 components kept as cardiac, only
**4.5 % have an index below 10**, and the median index is **50**. In **82 of 106
conditions there is nothing cardiac at all in the first ten singular vectors**.
A rank-6 or rank-10 truncation — the reflex when one thinks of the SVD as a
compression step — would discard the signal entirely. Rank 100 is not
conservatism; it is the minimum that reaches the pulse.

That the cardiac subspace is spread over dozens of components, rather than
concentrated in one pair, is also why a *combination* step exists at all: a
median of 30 of the 100 components peak inside the cardiac band, and 5 of them
(median) survive the concentration threshold to be mixed into the pulse.

## The seven methods

Hover (or tab to) any cell in the **what it does** column for the full sequence
of steps.

| | method | what it does | what it needs to know |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | no filter | <span class="method-hint" tabindex="0">the optimised combination, untouched<span class="method-pop"><strong>0 · no filter</strong><span class="pt">The rank-100 SVD of the pixel traces gives 100 temporal singular vectors.</span><span class="pt">The optimised spectral combination selects the cardiac ones and fits a weight for each.</span><span class="pt">Those weighted vectors are summed into a single pulse.</span><span class="pt">The pulse is resampled onto the uniform time grid, which the Hilbert transform requires.</span><span class="pt">Its sign is fixed against the phasor at the reference frequency — and nothing else is done.</span><span class="pt">Present only as a control: it shows what a phase looks like when no filtering is applied.</span></span></span> | — |
| 1 | FIR band-pass | <span class="method-hint" tabindex="0">linear-phase FIR over HR ± 20 %<span class="method-pop"><strong>1 · FIR band-pass</strong><span class="pt">Starts from the same combined pulse as method 0.</span><span class="pt">Interpolated from the true timestamps onto the uniform grid.</span><span class="pt">Band-passed by a linear-phase FIR whose band is the reference rate ± 20 %.</span><span class="pt">Linear phase means a constant group delay, so the filter shifts no frequency relative to another — the phase stays unbiased.</span><span class="pt">The first and last 20 % of samples are dropped from every statistic, to keep the filter transient out of the comparison.</span><span class="pt">This is the reference every other method is scored against.</span></span></span> | the reference HR |
| 2 | SSA on the pulse | <span class="method-hint" tabindex="0">singular spectrum analysis of the combined pulse, cardiac components regrouped<span class="method-pop"><strong>2 · SSA on the pulse</strong><span class="pt">Embeds the combined pulse in a Hankel trajectory matrix, window L = 3 cardiac cycles.</span><span class="pt">Takes the SVD of that matrix and examines its first 20 components.</span><span class="pt">Reconstructs each component as a 1-D signal by averaging its anti-diagonals.</span><span class="pt">Calls a component cardiac when its Lomb–Scargle peak falls within ± 20 % of the reference rate — a test, not a filter: no band is imposed on the signal.</span><span class="pt">Sums the components kept, typically 2, one oscillation showing up as a pair.</span><span class="pt">If none qualifies, falls back to the two carrying the most in-band power.</span></span></span> | HR, for grouping only |
| 3a | M-SSA | <span class="method-hint" tabindex="0">one trajectory matrix stacking all cardiac channels, then first PC<span class="method-pop"><strong>3a · M-SSA (multichannel)</strong><span class="pt">Builds one Hankel matrix per cardiac channel and stacks them vertically into a single tall matrix.</span><span class="pt">A single SVD therefore sees one temporal subspace shared by every channel — the physical hypothesis of the problem: one pulse, seen by several channels at different amplitudes and delays.</span><span class="pt">Diagonal-averages each component back, channel by channel.</span><span class="pt">Groups on the mean across channels: a component is cardiac or it is not, since that is a property of the shared mode.</span><span class="pt">Summing the kept components gives denoised channels which are near rank 2 by construction.</span><span class="pt">Their first principal component is the pulse.</span></span></span> | HR, for grouping only |
| 3b | SSA per channel | <span class="method-hint" tabindex="0">each channel denoised separately, then re-combined<span class="method-pop"><strong>3b · SSA per channel</strong><span class="pt">Runs method 2's SSA independently on each cardiac channel.</span><span class="pt">Each channel is therefore denoised on its own basis, with no assumption that they share a subspace — the opposite premise to M-SSA.</span><span class="pt">Feeds the denoised channels back into the optimised spectral combination.</span><span class="pt">The combination re-selects and re-weights them, exactly as it did on the raw singular vectors.</span><span class="pt">Costs one full SSA per channel, which is where its 3.4 s per condition come from.</span></span></span> | HR, for grouping only |
| — | DMD · model | <span class="method-hint" tabindex="0">BOPDMD rank 6; the retained mode evaluated analytically<span class="method-pop"><strong>DMD · model</strong><span class="pt">Takes the same normalised trace matrix, transposed to pyDMD's (space, time) convention.</span><span class="pt">Fits BOPDMD at rank 6 — three conjugate pairs — directly on the true, non-uniform timestamps.</span><span class="pt">Three initialisations are tried (default, harmonic seed, harmonic seed plus a purely-imaginary eigenvalue constraint) and the one landing closest to the reference rate is kept.</span><span class="pt">Eigenvalues are continuous-time here, so a mode's frequency is Im(λ)/2π — not log(λ) as for a discrete-time DMD.</span><span class="pt">The mode closest to the reference rate is retained and evaluated analytically as 2 Re(a e^(λt)).</span><span class="pt">Interpolated onto the uniform grid so its phase is comparable sample by sample with the others.</span></span></span> | HR, to pick the mode |
| — | DMD · projected | <span class="method-hint" tabindex="0">the same mode's coordinate obtained by projecting the data<span class="method-pop"><strong>DMD · projected</strong><span class="pt">Same fit and same retained mode as above — only the final step differs.</span><span class="pt">Instead of evaluating the model, the data are projected onto the mode basis: pinv(modes) applied to the trace matrix.</span><span class="pt">The row of those coordinates belonging to the retained mode is taken as the pulse.</span><span class="pt">It therefore keeps whatever the data actually do along that direction, noise included, rather than the clean exponential the fit prescribes.</span><span class="pt">That contrast is the point: the same mode, read as a model and read as a measurement.</span></span></span> | HR, to pick the mode |

Method 1 is the reference **by construction**, so its correlation of 1.00 with
itself in the tables below is a definition, not a finding. Methods 2, 3a and 3b
are the interesting comparison: they are data-adaptive, and use the heart rate
only to decide which SSA components are cardiac — never to impose a passband.

## One condition, seven pulses

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f1_pulses.qmd >}}

The dotted lines mark one cardiac period at the reference rate, so a
well-behaved pulse should cross zero on a regular grid. Reading top to bottom:

- **No filter** is not a pulse. Nothing periodic is visible above the noise.
- **FIR** and **SSA** are nearly the same trace, and both show a clear amplitude
  modulation — weak beats between 3 s and 7 s, strong ones after 8 s. This
  modulation is real signal, not a filtering artifact: it survives two
  independent methods.
- **M-SSA** flattens that modulation into a much more uniform oscillation. It is
  extracting the *shared* subspace across channels, and beat-to-beat amplitude
  is precisely what is not shared.
- **DMD · model** is a perfectly regular sinusoid. It has to be: a single DMD
  mode is $a e^{\lambda t}$, one frequency, one fixed initial phase. It cannot
  represent amplitude modulation, and it cannot drift with the heart rate.
- **DMD · projected** is noise.

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f2_spectra.qmd >}}

The spectra say the same thing more compactly: the unfiltered combination puts
most of its power outside the cardiac band, and the projected DMD coordinate
peaks well below it.

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f3_hr_inst.qmd >}}

## Is the phase interpretable at all?

The Hilbert transform returns a meaningful instantaneous phase only for a
narrow-band signal. When that condition is violated, the unwrapped phase *runs
backwards* — a negative instantaneous frequency, which has no physical reading
for a heartbeat. That fraction is a direct, assumption-free test of whether a
given pulse may be used for folding.

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f5_phase_legitimacy.qmd >}}

Unfiltered, **16 % of samples have a phase going backwards** and 83 % of them
sit outside the cardiac band. This is the quantitative justification for
filtering before taking any phase — without it, roughly one sample in six is
assigned to the wrong point of the cardiac cycle. Every filtered method brings
this below 1 %.

## Rate: accuracy and stability

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f6_hr_accuracy.qmd >}}

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/tab_methods.qmd >}}

Read that table with the caveat stated above. **DMD · model wins every rate
column** — 0.63 BPM from the reference, an interquartile range of 2.5 BPM — and
is nonetheless the second-worst method on this page. Its correlation with the
FIR pulse is **0.09**. A pure sinusoid at the correct frequency is not the same
object as the pulse: its phase is set once at $t = 0$ and never corrected, so
after a few tens of seconds of ordinary heart-rate variability it is
phase-incoherent with the actual heartbeat. It answers "what was the average
rate", which is not the question the pipeline asks.

The honest ranking for *phase* use is therefore: FIR, then SSA (correlation
0.95, at 3.5× the cost), then a clear gap to per-channel SSA (0.59) and M-SSA
(0.54). That SSA tracks the FIR band-pass this closely without being told a
passband is the substantive result — it means the band-pass is not imposing the
pulse, it is recovering one that is there.

## BOPDMD: initialisation is the whole method

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f8_dmd_init.qmd >}}

With default initialisation (B1), BOPDMD lands within ±20 % of the reference
heart rate in **3 % of conditions**. Seeded with the cardiac fundamental and its
harmonics (B2) it reaches **91 %**; adding the purely-imaginary eigenvalue
constraint (B3) reaches **100 %**, with a median error of 0.31 BPM.

The eigenvalue plane explains the failure. B1's modes collapse toward zero
frequency — it spends its rank-6 budget on the same low-frequency drift that
dominates the leading singular vectors. B2 and B3 sit tightly on 1×, 2× and 3×
the reference rate: at rank 6, three conjugate pairs, BOPDMD recovers the
fundamental and two harmonics, which is a sensible description of a pulse
waveform.

This is worth stating plainly: **BOPDMD did not find the cardiac frequency, it
was told where to look**, and the 100 % figure for B3 measures the quality of
the prior, not the discovery power of the method. Two further caveats belong
here — the variational-projection solver reported a non-convergence warning on
**every** fit across all three variants, and the mode is selected *a posteriori*
as the one closest to the known heart rate.

## What it costs

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f7_cost_fidelity.qmd >}}

Three orders of magnitude separate the methods, and cost does not buy fidelity.
FIR costs 7 ms; SSA 25 ms for a correlation of 0.95; per-channel SSA costs
3.4 s — 480× the FIR — for a correlation of 0.59. BOPDMD costs about 1.8 s per
condition and yields, for phase purposes, nothing.

## Choosing the SSA window

The one free parameter of the SSA methods is the embedding window $L$, set here
in cardiac cycles rather than samples so it adapts to each subject's rate.

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f9_ssa_sweep.qmd >}}

Below 2 cycles the window cannot resolve the fundamental: in-band power collapses
to 68 % and the rate scatters over 13.5 BPM. From 3 cycles on the curves flatten,
and the two approaches part company. For **SSA on the pulse**, 3 and 5 cycles are
nearly indistinguishable (rate IQR 7.3 vs 6.9 BPM) while the grouping stops being
clean above 3 — the number of components tagged cardiac climbs from 2 to 4, then
6 at 8 cycles, meaning the decomposition is splitting the same oscillation across
more components. **3 cycles remains the right default there**, and it is what
every other result on this page uses. **M-SSA is a different story**: it improves
markedly out to 5 cycles (IQR 10.3 → 7.9 BPM), which is consistent with it
needing a longer window to lock onto a subspace shared across channels. Since
M-SSA loses on waveform fidelity anyway, this was not pursued.

## What did not work

{{< include figures_pulse_from_data/f10_outcome.qmd >}}

**106 of the 107 conditions now produce a result.** That figure is recent: an
earlier pass over the same data returned only 81, and the 26 missing conditions
were lost to two guards in the trace builder rather than to anything wrong with
the recordings.

Registration can leave a frame blank, or reduce its choroid mask to a sliver.
Two consequences followed, both fixed:

- **19 conditions, "all-NaN traces"** — per-frame intensity normalisation divides
  each frame by its own mean. A blank frame has mean zero, so the division
  poisoned that row with NaN, and a single bad frame was enough to make the whole
  SVD input non-finite. Such a frame is now left at zero instead.
- **7 conditions, "empty ROI"** — the ROI keeps only pixels inside the mask in
  *every* frame, so one degenerate frame emptied the intersection and no trace
  survived. Frames whose mask covers less than 30 % of the temporal median area
  are now excluded from that intersection; they keep their place in the time
  base and simply lose their vote on the pixel set.

The 30 % threshold is not tuned to rescue conditions: across the cohort, the
smallest per-frame mask of a *healthy* recording sits at 0.50 of its own median
(0.84 median across conditions), while degenerate frames sit at or near 0. Of the
81 conditions that already worked, exactly one changed — and it *gained* usable
pixels, its ROI having been clipped by two bad frames out of 457.

**One condition still fails**, and for a different reason: its masks never
overlap enough to leave a stable ROI, even after degenerate frames are removed.
That is a registration or segmentation problem, not a missing guard, and no
threshold on mask area fixes it.

Two smaller caveats: the concentration threshold had to be lowered below its
nominal 0.15 in **49 of 106 conditions** for the combination to select any
channel at all — a higher share than before, since the newly recovered
conditions are the harder ones. And all methods are scored against a band centred
on the reference HR, so the comparison measures agreement with a known rate
rather than blind discovery.

## Conclusion

- The cardiac signal lives at **high singular indices** (median 50, essentially
  never below 10). Rank-100 decomposition is a requirement, not a safety margin.
- **Unfiltered phase is not usable**: one sample in six runs backwards.
- **The FIR band-pass remains the right default** — cheapest, cleanest phase.
  **SSA is the credible alternative**, reproducing it at 0.95 correlation
  without being handed a passband, at 3.5× the cost. Use it as an independent
  check that the band-pass is not manufacturing the pulse it finds.
- **M-SSA and per-channel SSA are not worth their cost** for phase; M-SSA
  actively destroys the beat-to-beat amplitude modulation, and it is the method
  that degraded most when the harder conditions were added (correlation 0.66 on
  the easy 81, 0.54 on all 106).
- **BOPDMD is a rate estimator, not a phase estimator.** With harmonic
  initialisation and an imaginary-eigenvalue constraint it returns the heart rate
  to a median 0.31 BPM of the reference — never worse than 1.6 BPM on any of the
  106 conditions — and a phase that correlates 0.09 with the real pulse. If an
  average rate is what is wanted, it is excellent; for folding, it cannot be
  used.
